n: Israel is a vine that produces fruit only for itself. As prosperity grew, so did their altars and sacred pillars—they used God’s blessings to serve idols.

f.g: Fine sacred pillars used in idol worship.

n: Their heart is divided—or “slippery,” deceitful. They must bear their guilt, and God will tear down their altars and smash their pillars.
Soon they will say, “We have no king, because we did not fear the Lord—and what could a king do for us anyway?” Their political system has collapsed in futility.
Their promises are empty, their treaties made with false oaths. Lawsuits spring up like poisonous weeds in a plowed field.
Samaria’s people will tremble for the calf idol at Beth-aven (Bethel). Its priests will wail as its glory is carried away.

f.g: Hebrew kemarim—a word used only for idol priests.

n: The calf will be carried to Assyria as a gift for the great king. What Israel worshipped becomes tribute for its conqueror—Ephraim will be put to shame.
Samaria’s king will float away like a twig on water—powerless and gone.

f.w: as the foam upon the water
f.g: Like a chip of wood or foam swept away.

n: The shrines of wickedness will be destroyed and overgrown with thorns. People will beg the mountains to cover them and the hills to fall on them—words Jesus and John later used for future judgment.

f.w: they shall say to the mountains, Cover us; and to the hills, Fall on us

n: Since the days of Gibeah, Israel has kept on sinning. Gibeah’s war against the wicked didn’t stop sin from continuing in Israel.
God will discipline them when He chooses; nations will gather against them for their “double guilt.”

f.g: Probably “their double iniquity”; the Hebrew is uncertain.

n: Ephraim was like a trained heifer that enjoyed threshing grain—easy work where she could eat freely. Now God will put a yoke on her neck for hard plowing. Judah and Jacob will labor too.

f.w: loveth to tread out the corn
f.g: Threshing oxen could eat as they worked.

f.w: I passed over upon her fair neck
f.g: I will put a yoke on her neck.

n: A beautiful call to repentance: sow righteousness, reap the fruit of loyal love, break up the hard, unplowed ground of your hearts. It is time to seek the Lord until He comes and showers righteousness on you.

f.g: Plow unused, hardened soil—soften your hearts.

f.w: it is time to seek the LORD

n: Instead, they plowed wickedness and reaped injustice, eating the fruit of lies, because they trusted in their own way and their army.

f.w: Ye have plowed wickedness, ye have reaped iniquity
the multitude of thy mighty men

n: War will break out, and all their fortresses will fall—like Shalman’s brutal destruction of Beth-arbel, where mothers and children were dashed to pieces. The event is otherwise unknown; Shalman may be a Moabite king or an Assyrian ruler.

f.g: Possibly Shalmaneser V of Assyria or Salamanu, a Moabite king; uncertain.
A town, perhaps in Gilead; location uncertain.

n: This will happen because of Bethel’s great wickedness. At dawn the king of Israel will be completely cut off—fulfilled when Hoshea, Israel’s last king, was taken prisoner by Assyria.

f.w: the king of Israel utterly be cut off
